chunks: He said to me: “Delay the Maghrib a little, for the sun sets where you are before it sets where we are.”
(1031) 68 — From him, from Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Waḍḍāḥ, who said:

I wrote to al-ʿAbd al-Ṣāliḥ عليه السلام: “The disk disappears and the night approaches, then the night increases in rising, and the sun becomes hidden from us, while a redness rises above the mountain, and the mu’adhdhins give the adhan among us. Should I pray at that time and break my fast if I am fasting, or should I wait until the redness above the mountain goes away?” So he wrote back to me: “I consider it proper for you to wait until the redness goes away and to take precaution for your religion.”

So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the reports we presented earlier, because his statement عليه السلام in the first report, “Delay the Maghrib,” means until the redness disappears from the eastern side; and likewise his statement in the second report. We have already indicated that through the earlier reports, and what further clarifies it is what he narrated:
As for what was narrated by al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad ibn Samāʿah, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Yaʿqūb ibn Shuʿayb, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:

key_terms.اللَّيْلُ: nightfall as it begins to appear
key_terms.الْحَائِطَةِ: precaution and safeguarding in religious practice
key_terms.الْمَغْرِبِ: the time of Maghrib salat at sunset
key_terms.حُمْرَةٌ: the redness or twilight glow remaining after sunset

ai.seo_question: When should Maghrib salat and iftar be performed if the sun has set but the redness remains above the horizon?
ai.summary: This passage addresses the legal timing of Maghrib salat and breaking the fast when the sun has disappeared but the twilight redness remains visible. It indicates that one should wait until the redness is gone, taking precaution in matters of religion, and explains that the reports are understood consistently in that light.
